questions.prompt: What is continuous integration, at its core?

options.text: Deploying to production once a year
Automatically building and testing every change so breakage is caught early
Writing tests only before a release
Running tests manually on your laptop

questions.explanation: CI verifies each change automatically with a self-testing build, catching integration problems within minutes.

questions.prompt: Why run lint/type-check before the full test run in a pipeline?

options.text: They're fast and cheap, so obvious problems fail in seconds (fail-fast)
They replace the need for tests

questions.explanation: Ordering fast checks first surfaces obvious failures quickly, saving time before the slower test run.

questions.prompt: Which keep CI fast and trustworthy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stage slow/E2E tests instead of running all on every push
Mask flaky tests with blanket reruns
Gate merges on green required checks

questions.explanation: Parallelism, caching, staging, and required checks help; blanket reruns hide flakiness and erode trust.

questions.prompt: A CI check that must pass before a pull request can merge is called a required ____ check.
questions.explanation: Required status checks gate merges so broken changes can't reach the shared branch.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a typical CI pipeline.

items.text: Checkout code and set up the runtime

questions.explanation: Check out and set up, install deps, run fast checks first, then the test suite.

questions.prompt: Match each CI technique to its benefit.

pairs.right: Run tests concurrently to cut wall-clock time
Avoid repeating slow installs each run
Fast tests per push, slow tests less often
Block merges while tests are red

questions.explanation: These techniques keep feedback fast and the shared branch releasable.
